D.comparison: Small set of a priori motivational constructs

O.outcome_detail: Explanatory adequacy for situated motivated action

cells.quote: A currently common motivational approach would employ a small, a priori set of constructs—Maya’s self-efficacy, or her perceived task value and cost, or her achievement goals, or interest, or controlled and autonomous regulations, or sense of belonging. Each of these may afford some insight. But specifying a small set of constructs in advance as the explanatory core for the phenomenon of Maya’s situated actions risks three possible failures. First, it may fail to capture other constructs that prove highly relevant to Maya’s experience in this instance. Second, it is likely to obscure the complexity, dynamics, and variability of the processes that give rise to situated motivated action for a particular person in a particular situation. And third, a focus on individuals’ motivation constructs tends to background the contextual, social, and situated features that are central to situated motivated action.
cells.note: The direction is the authors' theoretical claim that the Complex Dynamic Systems approach avoids limitations of the comparison; no empirical effect size or new data are reported.

D.treatment: ASSISTments with minimalist intelligence and adaptivity
D.comparison: systems with strong student models and sophisticated adaptation

cells.quote: Unlike other systems presented in this volume, ASSITments follows a rather minimalist approach when it comes to intelligence and adaptivity. It does not support a strong student model and does not implement a sophisticated adaptation procedure. Yet, the practical success of ASSISTments demonstrates that “a little intelligence can go a long way."
cells.note: The study text presents this as an editorial interpretation rather than a direct comparative evaluation; it does not report a statistical effect or specify learner expertise, age, or duration.

D.comparison: single- or dual-disciplinary Groups A and C works

O.outcome_detail: peer ratings of entertainment, relevance, and effectiveness

cells.quote: Notably, Group B, which employed a multiple interdisciplinary composition, attained the highest mean scores in all three criteria: entertainment (9.00 ± 1.30), relevance (9.08 ± 1.11), and effectiveness (9.15 ± 1.00). By comparison, Group A (single-disciplinary, Medicine only) and Group C (dual-disciplinary) showed lower scores across all dimensions, with similar performance levels between the two groups. However, no statistically significant differences were observed between the groups.
cells.note: The student works were produced in one classroom session and evaluated by peers; the text does not state random assignment or provide an equivalence test or power analysis.
